prompt: `go version` prints `go version go1.22.4 linux/amd64` on your machine. What does that tell you before lesson 1 goes any further?
hint: Compare with the release the transcripts were recorded with.

choices.text: An older release than the course's 1.27.1 is first in `PATH`
choices.why: Right. Either the new install did not happen or another `go` is found first; `command -v go` names the file that runs.

choices.text: Go is not installed and the shell guessed a version
choices.why: A missing `go` is `command not found`, exit 127. Something answered here.

choices.text: The machine is not Linux
choices.why: `linux/amd64` says it is.

choices.text: Everything is fine: any 1.x release behaves the same for a web server
choices.why: The 1.22 routing in this very lesson did not exist before 1.22, and later lessons use newer additions still.

prompt: Why does this course recommend installing Go on your own computer rather than using the Go Playground?
hint: What does the course type besides Go code?

choices.text: The Playground runs an older Go
choices.why: The release is not the problem the section names.

choices.text: The Playground charges for programs that open ports
choices.why: It costs nothing; it simply has no terminal.

choices.text: A server needs a terminal beside it to send requests from, and the Playground has none
choices.why: Right. It shows one program's output; there is nowhere to type `curl`.

choices.text: A virtual machine is required by Go 1.27
choices.why: A virtual machine is one of the three paths, not a requirement.

prompt: In `hello`, the handler is registered with the pattern `"/"`. Which requests does it answer?
hint: A pattern ending in a slash claims a subtree.

choices.text: Only `GET /`
choices.why: That is `GET /{$}`. A bare `/` with no method matches everything below it, whatever the method.

choices.text: Only the path `/`, with any method
choices.why: The trailing slash makes it a subtree, the whole site.

choices.text: Every path, with every method
choices.why: Right. `/events/7` and `POST /anything` reached it too.

choices.text: Every `GET`, and other methods get 405
choices.why: There is no method in the pattern, so no method is refused.

prompt: What does `ListenAndServe` return when the server is working?
hint: Why is it wrapped in `log.Fatal`?

choices.text: Nothing until it fails
choices.why: Right. It returns only with an error, and `log.Fatal` prints it and exits.

choices.text: A `*Server` value the program keeps and later uses to stop it
choices.why: It returns an error and nothing else; the `*Server` is something you build yourself in section 08.

choices.text: nil, straight after the port is open
choices.why: Then `log.Fatal(nil)` would end the program the moment it started.

choices.text: A running count of the requests it has served so far
choices.why: No such count exists in its signature: `func ListenAndServe(addr string, handler Handler) error`.

prompt: `go run .` prints `listen tcp 127.0.0.1:8080: bind: address already in use`. What is the likeliest cause on a laptop?
hint: Who else would want port 8080?

choices.text: A firewall rule on the laptop is blocking every connection to port 8080
choices.why: A firewall filters traffic; it does not make `bind` fail with this message.

choices.text: The handler panicked
choices.why: No request had arrived; the program failed while opening the port.

choices.text: An earlier copy of it, still running
choices.why: Right. One program per port; stop the old one with Ctrl+C, or find it with `ss -ltnp`.

choices.text: `localhost` is not allowed as an address
choices.why: It is allowed, and the message shows it resolved to `127.0.0.1`.

prompt: Why does every program after section 03 build its own mux instead of passing `nil`?
hint: What else can register on `DefaultServeMux`?

choices.text: `nil` is slower
choices.why: Speed is not the argument; `nil` simply means the package's shared mux.

choices.text: `DefaultServeMux` ignores the 1.22 patterns
choices.why: It is a `ServeMux` like any other and understands them.

choices.text: Imported packages add routes to it, as `net/http/pprof` does
choices.why: Right. With a mux of its own, the routes a server answers are the ones `main` registered.

choices.text: Passing `nil` as the handler makes the server listen on every network interface of the machine
choices.why: The address decides that; the handler argument has nothing to do with it.

prompt: What makes a type an `http.Handler`?
hint: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly.

choices.text: Embedding `http.Handler` in the struct
choices.why: That would give it a nil handler to call. A method of its own is what is needed.

choices.text: Registering it with `http.Handle`, which checks the type and turns it into a handler
choices.why: `Handle` accepts only what is already a handler; it does not make one.

choices.text: A method `ServeHTTP(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request)`
choices.why: Right. The method set is the whole requirement; nothing is declared.

choices.text: An `implements http.Handler` comment above the type
choices.why: Go has no `implements`, in code or in comments.

prompt: `mux.Handle("/hello", http.HandlerFunc(hello))` and `mux.HandleFunc("/hi", hello)`: what is the difference between the two registrations?
hint: `HandlerFunc` is a type.

choices.text: The first runs `hello` in a new goroutine and the second does not
choices.why: The server starts one goroutine per request either way.

choices.text: Only the path; `HandleFunc` does the same conversion for you
choices.why: Right. Both end up registering an `http.HandlerFunc` wrapping `hello`.

choices.text: The second copies `hello` for each request
choices.why: A function value is not copied per request; it is called.

choices.text: The first does not compile: a function is not a handler
choices.why: The conversion to `http.HandlerFunc` gives it the method; it compiled and answered.

prompt: The three `curl` calls to `/visits` came one after another and the count was right. Why does `visits` still lock a mutex?
hint: How does `net/http` run requests?

choices.text: To make the numbers come out in the terminal in the order the requests were sent
choices.why: Order in a terminal is not what a lock protects; it protects `v.n` from two writers.

choices.text: Because `ServeHTTP` on a pointer receiver will not compile without one
choices.why: It compiles without one, and races without one.

choices.text: Requests run concurrently, one goroutine each
choices.why: Right. Correct only when requests take turns is not correct.

choices.text: `fmt.Fprintf` to a `ResponseWriter` is not safe without a lock
choices.why: Each request has its own writer; the shared thing is the counter.

prompt: A `*ServeMux` can be registered inside another mux, because it has a method called ___.
hint: The one method of `http.Handler`.

prompt: In the pattern `GET /events/{id}`, what does `r.PathValue("id")` return for a request to `/events/42`?
hint: Look at the type `PathValue` returns.

choices.text: The int `42`
choices.why: The mux knows nothing of numbers; converting is the handler's job.

choices.text: The string `"42"`
choices.why: Right. `strconv.Atoi` turns it into a number, and its error is the handler's 400.

choices.text: The whole path, `/events/42`
choices.why: That is `r.URL.Path`; `PathValue` returns the one segment the wildcard took.

choices.text: An empty string until `r.ParseForm` is called
choices.why: Path values are set by the mux before the handler runs; forms are another matter.

prompt: `curl -X DELETE localhost:8080/events` gets `405 Method Not Allowed` with `Allow: GET, HEAD, POST`. Who wrote that `Allow` header?
hint: Nobody in `routes/main.go` mentions `HEAD`.

choices.text: `curl`, which guessed it
choices.why: It printed what the server sent.

choices.text: The mux, from the methods registered for that path
choices.why: Right, with `HEAD` added because a `GET` pattern answers it too.

choices.text: The handler for `GET /events`
choices.why: No handler ran: the method matched no pattern for that path.

choices.text: The operating system's network stack
choices.why: HTTP status codes are above anything the kernel knows about.

prompt: Match each pattern to a request it answers and the others do not.
hint: One segment, the rest of the path, or exactly the end.

prompt: Why does `GET /about` answer 404 in `routes`, when `GET /` would have answered it?
hint: What does `{$}` add?

choices.text: `/about` is reserved by `net/http`
choices.why: No path is reserved; no pattern here matched it.

choices.text: Patterns are matched in the order they were registered, and `/about` came too late
choices.why: Registration order plays no part in `ServeMux`.

choices.text: Wildcards need at least one segment, and `/about` has none
choices.why: There is no wildcard in `GET /{$}`, and `/about` has one segment.

choices.text: `{$}` makes the home pattern match `/` and stop there
choices.why: Right. Without it, a pattern ending in a slash is a subtree and catches `/about`.

prompt: A client that does not follow redirects calls `GET /static` on `routes` and reports an error. What did it receive?
hint: `/static` is not under `/static/`.

choices.text: A 404, because `/static` is not registered
choices.why: The mux knows a subtree exists one slash away and says so.

choices.text: A 405, because the pattern has no method
choices.why: A pattern with no method accepts every method.

choices.text: A 200 with an empty body from the `/static/` handler
choices.why: The handler did not run; the mux answered before it.

choices.text: A 307 with `Location: /static/`
choices.why: Right. Helpful for a directory, surprising for an API client.

prompt: Both `GET /events/{id}` and `GET /events/latest` are registered. Which one answers `/events/latest`?
hint: Which one matches fewer requests?

choices.text: Whichever was registered first
choices.why: That is how many routers work, and not `ServeMux`.

choices.text: Whichever was registered last
choices.why: Order plays no part.

choices.text: Neither: the program panics at start
choices.why: They overlap, but one is more specific, so there is no conflict.

choices.text: The literal one, wherever it sits in the file
choices.why: Right. It matches a strict subset of what the wildcard matches, so it is more specific.

prompt: Why does `conflict` panic instead of picking a handler for `/events/42`?
hint: Read the third and fourth lines of the message.

choices.text: Neither is more specific than the other
choices.why: Right. The mux refuses at registration rather than guess at request time.

choices.text: A wildcard may not be the first segment of a pattern
choices.why: `/{kind}/42` is allowed on its own; the problem is the pair.

choices.text: Both patterns name the method `GET`, and one method may only appear once per mux
choices.why: Many patterns share a method. Overlap with no winner is the problem.

choices.text: `42` is a number and patterns only hold text
choices.why: `42` in a pattern is literal text, and that is fine.

prompt: An old service moves to a `go.mod` saying `go 1.21`, and every route with a method in it starts answering 404. What happened?
hint: The `go` line decides which mux behaviour you get.

choices.text: The old mux reads `GET /events` as a literal path, which no request ever has
choices.why: Right. Below `go 1.22`, or with `GODEBUG=httpmuxgo121=1`, methods and wildcards are just text.

choices.text: Go 1.21 cannot compile `HandleFunc`
choices.why: `HandleFunc` is as old as the package; it compiled.

choices.text: The server now refuses every method except `GET`
choices.why: A refused method would be 405, not 404, and `GET` fails too.

choices.text: The patterns conflict under 1.21 and are silently dropped
choices.why: Nothing is dropped; they are registered as literal paths.

prompt: A handler writes the body first and then calls `w.Header().Set("X-Seats", "40")`. What does the client receive?
hint: The order of an HTTP response.

choices.text: The body, and `X-Seats: 40` at the end of it
choices.why: Headers do not travel after the body in an ordinary response.

choices.text: A 500, because the header came too late
choices.why: The 200 had already gone; nothing can replace it.

choices.text: A compile error
choices.why: Nothing about call order is checked by the compiler.

choices.text: The body, and no `X-Seats` header
choices.why: Right. The first write sent the headers; later changes to the map go nowhere.

prompt: The server prints `http: superfluous response.WriteHeader call from main.main.func2 (main.go:20)`. What does it mean?
hint: Which call is superfluous, and why?

choices.text: Line 20 set a status after one was sent
choices.why: Right. A write had sent 200 on its own; the second status went nowhere.

choices.text: Line 20 is unreachable code
choices.why: It ran; that is why it was reported.

choices.text: The handler set a status code that does not exist
choices.why: 202 exists. It came too late.

choices.text: Two different handlers were registered for the same path and both of them ran
choices.why: That would be a conflict panic at start, not a line per request.

prompt:
`/sniffed` sets no `Content-Type` and writes `

boxoffice

`. Why does the response say `text/html`?
hint: `http.DetectContentType`.

choices.text: `fmt.Fprint` marks its output as HTML
choices.why: `fmt` knows nothing about content types.

choices.text: It guessed from the first bytes
choices.why: Right. With no type set, it sniffs up to 512 bytes; a JSON API sets its own.

choices.text: `curl` added the header on its side when it saw the angle brackets
choices.why: `-i` prints what the server sent.

choices.text: Every `GET` defaults to HTML
choices.why: `hello` answered a `GET` with `text/plain`; the bytes decided.

prompt: What is the line right after `http.Error(w, "no such event", http.StatusNotFound)` in a handler, and why?
hint: `http.Error` is an ordinary function call.

choices.text: `w.WriteHeader(404)`, to make sure the status is sent
choices.why: `http.Error` sent it already; a second call is the superfluous line.

choices.text: `panic`, so that the server logs the failure
choices.why: A panic is for the impossible, not for a missing event.

choices.text: `return`, because `http.Error` does not stop the handler
choices.why: Right. Without it the code below runs and writes after the error.

choices.text: Nothing; `http.Error` returns from the handler itself
choices.why: No function can return from its caller in Go.

prompt: What timeouts does a server started with `http.ListenAndServe(addr, h)` have?
hint: The zero value of each field.

choices.text: None
choices.why: Right. Zero means no deadline, for reading, writing and idling.

choices.text: Thirty seconds for everything
choices.why: No such default exists in `net/http`.

choices.text: Whatever the operating system sets for TCP
choices.why: The kernel's keepalive is not a deadline on an HTTP request; the held connection stayed open.

choices.text: A read timeout, but no write timeout
choices.why: The connection held by hand proved there was no read deadline either.

prompt: Which field defends a server against a client that sends half a request and then waits?
hint: The connection held in this section never finished its headers.

choices.text: `IdleTimeout`
choices.why: Idle is the gap between requests on a kept-alive connection.

choices.text: `WriteTimeout`
choices.why: Its clock starts after the headers were read, which never happened.

choices.text: `MaxHeaderBytes`
choices.why: That limits size, and a slow client sends very little.

choices.text: `ReadHeaderTimeout`
choices.why: Right. Two seconds, and the server closed the connection.

prompt: Against `patient`, after how many seconds did the server close the half-sent request?
hint: The last line of the capture.

prompt: A handler streams a report that takes 25 seconds, on a server with `WriteTimeout: 10 * time.Second`. What happens?
hint: When does the write clock start, and what happens when it runs out?

choices.text: The server waits, because the handler is still writing
choices.why: The deadline is a deadline; writing does not extend it.

choices.text: The client receives a 408 Request Timeout
choices.why: The status went out long before; the connection is simply cut.

choices.text: The handler's context is cancelled at ten seconds and it returns cleanly
choices.why: `WriteTimeout` is a deadline on the connection, and the handler is not told.

choices.text: The response is cut off about ten seconds after the headers were read
choices.why: Right. Set it above the slowest response, or lift it for that route, as lesson 13 does.

prompt: In boxoffice, `/events/nine` answers 400 and `/events/9` answers 404. Why two different statuses?
hint: What was wrong with each request?

choices.text: `nine` is no id; `9` is nobody's
choices.why: Right. One is a malformed request, the other a missing resource.

choices.text: The mux refuses words in a wildcard
choices.why: The mux took `nine` happily; `strconv.Atoi` refused it.

choices.text: 404 is for numbers above 2
choices.why: It is for ids the store does not hold, whatever their size.

choices.text: The 400 is produced by `curl` before sending, and the 404 by the server
choices.why: Both came from `getEvent`.

prompt: Why does `memStore.List` sort the events before returning them?
hint: Where do they come from?

choices.text: Sorting makes the lock shorter
choices.why: It makes it longer, if anything.

choices.text: A map has no order of its own
choices.why: Right. An API that lists the same data in two orders is a bug report waiting.

choices.text: `fmt.Fprintf` needs sorted input
choices.why: It prints whatever it is given.

choices.text: The mux expects the ids it serves to arrive in ascending order
choices.why: The mux never sees the store.

prompt: Put what happens to one request to boxoffice in order, from the connection to the bytes the client reads.
hint: The mux is a handler that calls another handler.
items: The server accepts the connection and reads the headers within `ReadHeaderTimeout`
The server calls the mux's `ServeHTTP` in a goroutine for this request
The mux picks the most specific pattern and fills in `{id}`
The first write sends status 200 and the headers, then the body
trap: The status leaves with the first write, not when the handler returns.

prompt: A new route `GET /events/{id}/seats` is added to boxoffice. What does `curl -X POST localhost:8080/events/1/seats` get?
hint: The path exists; does the method?

choices.text: 404 page not found
choices.why: The path matches a registered pattern, so the mux knows it exists.

choices.text: The `GET` handler runs, because `POST` falls back to it
choices.why: Methods do not fall back to each other; only `HEAD` rides on `GET`.

choices.text: 405 with `Allow: GET, HEAD`
choices.why: Right. The path is known and only `GET`, with its `HEAD`, is registered for it.

choices.text: A panic, because the new pattern conflicts with `GET /events/{id}`
choices.why: They do not overlap: one segment after `/events/` against two.
